Common correlated effects for panels with unobserved common factors

Source: R/dpnl.R
ccepnl.Rd

The common correlated effects estimators of Pesaran (2006) for a panel whose errors hold unobserved common factors with unit-specific loadings, correlated with the regressors: the dependent variable and the regressors averaged across units in each period (with the weights w) are added to each unit's regression, with the observed common factors d_t (a constant, with cons = TRUE, and the columns of fac). With H = (D, ybar_w, Xbar_w) and M = I - H (H'H)^- H' (eq 15, a generalized inverse), the unit estimates are b_i = (X_i'M X_i)^-1 X_i'M y_i. The mean group estimator CCEMG is their mean (eq 53), with the nonparametric variance sum (b_i - b_MG)(b_i - b_MG)' / (N (N - 1)) (eq 58). The pooled estimator CCEP is (sum w_i X_i'M X_i)^-1 sum w_i X_i'M y_i, the pooling weights equal to the averaging weights as Theorem 3 requires, with the variance of eqs 67-69, sum w_i^2 Psi^-1 R Psi^-1, Psi = sum w_i X_i'M X_i / T and R = sum wt_i^2 (X_i'M X_i / T) (b_i - b_MG)(b_i - b_MG)' (X_i'M X_i / T) / (N - 1), wt_i = w_i / sqrt(mean(w^2)). Inference is normal.

Usage

ccepnl(
  y,
  x,
  unit,
  time,
  fac = NULL,
  cons = TRUE,
  w = NULL,
  avg = NULL,
  ylag = 0,
  lags = NULL,
  bias = "none",
  pool = NULL,
  pvar = "pesaran",
  level = 0.95
)

# S3 method for class 'ccepnl'
plot(x, ..., main = NULL, col = NULL, pal = NULL)

Arguments

y

The count of each row (a unit in a period): numbers from 0.

x

The regressors: a numeric matrix or data frame, one row per row of y. For plot(), a ccepnl result.

unit

The unit of each row: labels.

time

The period of each row: numbers; each unit at most once per period.

fac

NULL or observed common factors: a numeric matrix or data frame, one row per row of y, constant within each period.

cons

TRUE (default) for a constant among the observed factors, unit-specific intercepts.

w

NULL (equal weights 1 / N, as Pesaran 2006, sec. 5.2, says is typical) or a positive weight of each row, constant within each unit; they are scaled to sum to 1 over the units.

avg

NULL (default: the averages of y and of every column of x, Pesaran's choice) or the averages kept among the columns of H: "y" and names of columns of x.

ylag

The lags of y among the regressors: a whole number from 0 (default 0, the static model of Pesaran 2006).

lags

NULL (default: 0 for the static model, the integer part of T^(1/3) with ylag > 0) or the lags of the averages: a whole number from 0.

bias

"none" (default), "jack" (half-panel jackknife) or "rma" (recursive mean adjustment): the correction of the mean group estimate, as above.

pool

NULL (default: CCEP for the static model only), TRUE or FALSE: whether to make CCEP; TRUE is refused with ylag > 0 or bias.

pvar

"pesaran" (default, eqs 67-69 of Pesaran 2006) or "bsw" (Brown, Schmidt and Wooldridge 2026): the variance of CCEP.

level

The confidence level of the intervals.

...

Passed to the base-graphics call.

main

NULL (a default title) or one string.

col

NULL (the palette) or colours.

pal

NULL (the session palette, see plotopt()) or a palette name for blpal().

Value

An object of class ccepnl, a list: mg and pooled, the CCEMG and CCEP estimates (term, est, se, z, p, lo, hi; pooled NULL when not made); mg0, the uncorrected mean group estimate with bias (NULL otherwise); bi, the unit estimates (units by regressors, corrected with bias); vmg, vp and vmg0, the variances; hb, the heterogeneity-bias test of CCEP (NULL without CCEP); nfac, the number of factors (er, thr, avg); fit, one row (units, periods, k, h the columns of H, n the rows of the regressions, lags, ylag); w, the weights by unit; bias; pvar; and level.

Details

Pesaran (2006) derives the estimators for a balanced panel. An unbalanced one is handled as standard implementations handle it (Ditzen 2018, p. 586, says only that xtdcce2 "supports unbalanced panels"; Su, Wang and Wang 2026, p. 2, that "calculating cross-sectional averages of the dependent variable and covariates remains straightforward in unbalanced panels"): the averages of a period are taken over the units observed in that period, their weights scaled to sum to 1 over those units, and each unit's regression runs over its own periods, with its rows of H. CCEMG and its variance are then as above. CCEP is (sum w_i X_i'M_i X_i)^-1 sum w_i X_i'M_i y_i, and in its variance each X_i'M_i X_i is divided by the unit's own number of periods, which is this function's reading of T there. On a balanced panel all of this is Pesaran's estimator. Su, Wang and Wang (2026, sec. 6.3, p. 20) compute CCE on unbalanced panels in the same way, after Zhou and Zhang (2016, eq 12), and caution (p. 2 and n. 7, p. 4) that when whether a unit is observed is related to its loadings and varies over time, the averages no longer proxy the factors well; the estimators for unbalanced panels with interactive effects of Czarnowske and Stammann (2026, Assumption 1 and Remark 1, p. 1309) likewise assume that the data are missing at random, which excludes selection related to the idiosyncratic errors. Neither paper gives a diagnostic or correction for CCE estimators, and this function makes none. A period observed for one unit only, or a unit with fewer periods than its regression needs (twice the regressors and lags of y, the averages kept with their lags and the observed factors), is refused by name.

Dynamic panels. With ylag > 0 the lags 1..ylag of y join the regressors (as L1.y, ...), and with lags = p the averages kept enter H with their lags 1..p as well: the cross-sectionally augmented regression of Chudik and Pesaran (2015, eq 24) for heterogeneous panels with a lagged dependent variable and weakly exogenous regressors (lags of x, as their eq 1 has, are columns of x). A unit's regression runs over the periods in which it is observed together with its ylag periods before, from the p + 1-th period on (eqs 25-26); the averages are those of every observed unit-period, as above. lags = NULL takes p = 0 for the static model and, with ylag > 0, the integer part of T^(1/3), T the periods, as Chudik and Pesaran recommend (sec. 5.2, eq 40, and p. 404: "we recommend setting pT = [T^1/3]"). The mean group estimator is the mean of the unit estimates (eq 27) with the nonparametric variance of eq 32 over N. Pooled dynamic CCE is not supported: Chudik and Pesaran (2015, n. 5) recall that with heterogeneous slopes "pooled estimators are inconsistent in the case of panel data models with lagged dependent variables" (Pesaran and Smith 1995), and their theory is that of the mean group estimator; pool = NULL (default) makes CCEP only for the static model, and pool = TRUE with ylag > 0 or with bias is refused.

bias corrects the mean group estimate for the small-T time-series bias as Chudik and Pesaran (2015, sec. 4.1) define the corrections. "jack" is the half-panel jackknife (sec. 4.1.1, the unnumbered equation after eq 32), 2 b_MG - (b_MG^a + b_MG^b) / 2, a and b the estimates over periods 1..[T/2] and [T/2]+1..T; each half is taken as a panel of its own, so that the lags of y and of the averages of its first rows come from inside the half, as "computed from the first half of the available time period" reads, with the same p. "rma" is recursive mean adjustment (sec. 4.1.2 and n. 13): y and each column of x less the mean of the unit's values in the periods before, y_it - (t - 1)^-1 sum_{s<t} y_is, a unit's first period dropped, and the estimator applied to these series, so that the lags of y are lags of the adjusted y and the averages are those of the adjusted values; observed factors are not adjusted (Ditzen 2018, p. 589, leaves the constant out). The paper states no variance for the corrected estimators: vmg is the nonparametric mean group variance (eq 32) applied to the corrected unit estimates (bi: 2 b_i - (b_i^a + b_i^b) / 2 for the jackknife, the estimates on the adjusted series for "rma"), and the uncorrected estimate and its variance are returned in mg0 and vmg0 for comparison.

Five lessons. Juodis and Reese (2026) draw five lessons for applied work. (1) The averages are factor estimates measured with error, which can bias the estimates and change their variance: results should be checked against the number and kind of averages (avg keeps a subset), and with slopes common to all units and T not small against N the intervals of CCEP are not centred without a bias correction, which this function does not make (sec. 3.1). nfac reports the number of factors that the averages kept identify, by the two regularized procedures of their appendix A.1 on a balanced panel: er, the eigenvalue ratio of Ahn and Horenstein (2013) on the averages normalised by Sigma^-1/2, Sigma = sum_i (Z_i - Zbar)'(Z_i - Zbar) / (N T) (Juodis 2022; steps 1-3, r_max the averages less one); thr, the number of eigenvalues of Zbar'Zbar / T at least 0.01 times the largest (Vogt et al. 2025; steps 1-2); and avg, the averages kept; NA where undefined. More averages than factors is the case in which the paper warns of extra bias; the regularized estimators themselves are not made. (2) A two-way fixed-effects estimator (fepnl()) may still be consistent and should be compared and tested. hb is their test of heterogeneity bias in CCEP (sec. 3.2, case study 2): delta_i = (X_i'M_i X_i - N^-1 sum_j X_j'M_j X_j) (b_i - b_MG), HB = delta' V^-1 delta with delta their mean and V = N^-2 sum delta_i delta_i', chi-squared on k degrees of freedom (stat, df, p); a rejection says that CCEP is biased by slopes that vary with the regressors. (3) Dynamic models need the dynamics of every observed variable specified, and a bias correction is recommended in short panels (sec. 3.3; ylag, lags, bias above). (4) The CIPS panel unit-root test does not test what CCE estimation needs; they recommend the CSB test of Pesaran et al. (2013) (sec. 3.4), which this package does not provide. (5) There is no general recipe for nonlinear models, where the average of y should not be among the proxies (sec. 3.5); this function is linear. For cross-sectional dependence in the residuals see pcdtst().

Fixed-T variance. Brown, Schmidt and Wooldridge (2026, eqs 12-14 and Theorem 1) show that CCEP is the pooled least-squares estimate of y on the regressors with the columns of H partialled out unit by unit, and that time-varying regressors d_t added to it get coefficients of exactly 0. Their fixed-T variance of CCEP, which counts the sampling error of the averages (sec. 5.4, eqs 36-40, with Psi = H and q_i = vec(Z_i - Zbar), 0 in the columns of the observed factors), is pvar = "bsw": A^-1 B A^-1 / N, A = N^-1 sum X_i'M X_i, B = N^-1 sum s_i s_i', s_i = X_i'M u_i - G'(I + K)[Psi (Psi'Psi)^-1 (x) M] q_i, u_i = y_i - X_i b, G = N^-1 sum u_i (x) (X_i - Xbar) and K the commutation matrix (eq 33); it is for the static pooled estimator with equal weights on a balanced panel, and refused otherwise.

The plot draws the CCEMG and, when made, CCEP estimates of each regressor with their intervals and returns what it drew.

References

Pesaran, M. H. (2006). Estimation and inference in large heterogeneous panels with a multifactor error structure. Econometrica, 74(4), 967-1012. doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2006.00692.x

Ditzen, J. (2018). Estimating dynamic common-correlated effects in Stata. The Stata Journal, 18(3), 585-617. doi:10.1177/1536867X1801800306

Su, L., Wang, F. and Wang, Y. (2026). Estimation and inference for unbalanced panel data models with interactive fixed effects. Journal of Econometrics, 255, 106222. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2026.106222

Juodis, A. and Reese, S. (2026). Five lessons for applied researchers from twenty years of common correlated effects estimation. Journal of Econometrics, 253, 106120. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2025.106120

Chudik, A. and Pesaran, M. H. (2015). Common correlated effects estimation of heterogeneous dynamic panel data models with weakly exogenous regressors. Journal of Econometrics, 188(2), 393-420. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2015.03.007

Brown, N. L., Schmidt, P. and Wooldridge, J. M. (2026). A simple reformulation of the common correlated effects model. Econometric Reviews, 45(5), 760-772. doi:10.1080/07474938.2026.2615434

Czarnowske, D. and Stammann, A. (2026). Inference in unbalanced panel data models with interactive fixed effects. Econometric Reviews, 45(9), 1306-1337. doi:10.1080/07474938.2026.2681519

Examples

# 30 provinces over 12 years, one unobserved factor in y and x
set.seed(9)
d <- expand.grid(year = 1:12, prov = paste0("p", 1:30))
f <- rnorm(12)[d$year]
g <- rnorm(30, 1)[as.integer(substring(d$prov, 2))]
d$x <- g * f + rnorm(360)
d$y <- 1 + 0.7 * d$x + g * f + rnorm(360)
r <- ccepnl(d$y, d["x"], d$prov, d$year)
r
#> ccepnl: common correlated effects, 30 units, 12 periods
#> mean group (CCEMG):
#>  term       est         se        z            p        lo        hi
#>     x 0.7534011 0.06556476 11.49095 1.464985e-30 0.6248965 0.8819056
#> pooled (CCEP):
#>  term       est         se        z            p        lo        hi
#>     x 0.7581987 0.06456047 11.74401 7.580526e-32 0.6316625 0.8847349
#> heterogeneity bias of CCEP: chi2(1) = 0.0165, p 0.898
r$nfac
#>  er thr avg 
#>   1   2   2 
# a dynamic panel: y depends on its lag; jackknife-corrected mean group
set.seed(10)
tt <- 40
d <- expand.grid(year = 1:tt, prov = paste0("p", 1:40))
f <- rnorm(tt)[d$year]
g <- rnorm(40, 1)[as.integer(substring(d$prov, 2))]
d$x <- g * f + rnorm(nrow(d))
d$y <- 0
for (i in which(d$year > 1)) {
  d$y[i] <- 0.5 * d$y[i - 1] + 0.7 * d$x[i] + g[i] * f[i] + rnorm(1)
}
ccepnl(d$y, d["x"], d$prov, d$year, ylag = 1, bias = "jack")
#> ccepnl: common correlated effects, 40 units, 40 periods, 1 lags of y, 3 of the averages
#> mean group (CCEMG, jack):
#>  term       est         se        z            p        lo        hi
#>  L1.y 0.5946119 0.04214017 14.11033 3.280167e-45 0.5120187 0.6772051
#>     x 0.6781777 0.06129760 11.06369 1.881911e-28 0.5580366 0.7983187
